A hand-cut soba house near Kaminarimon with an Aomori accent — the sake list is Aomori (田酒, 七力) and the 暮坪 items use Iwate’s 暮坪かぶ, a pungent turnip grated in place of wasabi. ⚠ NOTHING HERE CLEARS EITHER DIET. Every noodle is soba or udon, the tsuyu is soy and dashi, and the tempura is wheat batter. That is stated rather than worked around. ⚠ THE ONE ITEM WORTH UNDERSTANDING IS 焼酎そば湯割り at ¥600 — shochu cut with 蕎麦湯, the cloudy water the soba was boiled in. It is the same trap recorded at 玄蕎麦しんがり: a coeliac who has avoided every bowl on the board can still be caught by a drink, because nothing in the words 焼酎 or 湯割り says noodle. ⚠ AND ONE DISH IS ONLY A PARTIAL LOSS: 豚しゃぶ at ¥2,500 per head, pre-order only and from two people, is pork and vegetables cooked in water — no batter, no noodle. Shabu-shabu sauces are ponzu and goma-dare, both soy-based, so it turns entirely on whether the kitchen will serve it with salt and citrus instead. That is the question to ask here.

⚠ THE ONLY DISH HERE WITH NO NOODLE AND NO BATTER: pork and vegetables cooked in water at the table. That makes it the one thing on a soba-house menu a coeliac could plausibly eat — and it turns on the dipping sauce, since ponzu and goma-dare are both soy-based. Ask for salt and citrus. Requires advance booking and a minimum of two people.

⚠ A DRINK MADE OF THE NOODLE WATER. 蕎麦湯 is the cloudy water the soba was boiled in — so it carries the 打ち粉 and whatever wheat was in the noodles — and nothing in the name 焼酎そば湯割り reads as a hazard to someone who has carefully avoided the food menu. The same trap appears at 玄蕎麦しんがり.
Junmai sake is rice, water and koji only — no added alcohol. The coeliac caveat is that koji is occasionally grown on barley.
